result: Four cryo-EM structures of E. coli RelA bound to the 70S ribosome were obtained at 3.9-4.1 Å resolution, revealing RelA in different states: Structure I shows RelA bound via its C-terminal portion with disordered N-terminal domains in the absence of A-site tRNA; Structures II, III, and IV show well-resolved central and C-terminal RelA domains with cognate deacyl-tRNA bound to the A site, differing in conformations of RelA, A/R tRNA, the 30S subunit, and the L11 stalk.
evaluation: Claims C4, C27-C32 are well-supported by the cryo-EM data presented in the manuscript. The resolution values (3.9-4.1 Å) are documented with FSC curves (Figure 1—figure supplement 2E), and the structural differences between the four structures are clearly demonstrated through figures and detailed descriptions. The local resolution in the ribosome core being higher than average resolution is consistent with typical cryo-EM structures of ribosome complexes.

result: RelA adopts a boomerang-shaped conformation with a wingspan exceeding 100 Å when bound with deacyl-tRNA, wrapping around the A/R tRNA. The CCA end of the A/R tRNA pins the central TGS domain against the 30S subunit, positioning the (p)ppGpp-synthetase domain near the 30S spur.
evaluation: Claims C5-C7, C52, C62-C63 are supported by the structural data shown in Figures 1-4. The boomerang shape and wingspan measurement are directly observable in the structures, and the positioning of the TGS domain pinned by the CCA end is clearly demonstrated in Figure 3A-B with supporting cryo-EM density.

result: The C-terminal region of RelA, comprising the ACT and RIS domains, forms a superdomain that anchors RelA to the 70S ribosome at intersubunit bridge B1a. The ACT domain (aa 665-744) contains four β-strands covered by two α-helices and interacts with the A-site finger and ribosomal protein L16. The RIS domain (aa 585-660) contains a four-stranded β-sheet and short α-helix, bridging the large and small ribosomal subunits through interactions with the A-site finger and ribosomal protein S19.
evaluation: Claims C36-C50 are well-supported by the structural data presented in Figures 2 and supplementary figures. The domain boundaries, structural features, and specific interactions are clearly resolved in the cryo-EM maps (Figure 2—figure supplement 1). The identification of the RIS domain as a novel ribosome-binding domain is supported by both structural data and consistency with prior biochemical studies showing reduced RelA binding upon C-terminal domain mutation.

result: The TGS domain interacts with the 3' CCA end of deacylated A/R tRNA through specific residues (H432, P411, K412) that stabilize the CCA conformation. An amino acid attached at A76 would sterically clash with the β-sheet of TGS, explaining why charged tRNA cannot activate RelA. The A/R tRNA disrupts the dimerization interface of the isolated TGS domain, potentially contributing to RelA activation by stabilizing monomeric RelA.
evaluation: Claims C67-C71, C73, C75, C77 are supported by the structural data in Figure 3 and comparison with the isolated TGS domain structure. The specific interactions between TGS residues and the CCA end are clearly resolved. The steric clash argument for why charged tRNA cannot activate RelA is a reasonable inference from the structural data. However, C77 is somewhat speculative as it proposes a mechanism (monomer stabilization) that is not directly tested.

result: Three conformations of the ribosome and A/R tRNA were captured (Structures II, III, IV), revealing stepwise accommodation of tRNA into the A site coupled with progressive 30S subunit domain closure. The acceptor arm of A/R tRNA and TGS domain shift ~2 Å between each structure, while the 30S shoulder moves nearly 5 Å from Structure II to IV. Structure II represents a previously unseen open 30S conformation with A-site tRNA present, Structure III shows an intermediate state, and Structure IV shows the fully closed conformation.
evaluation: Claims C8, C92, C96-C110 are well-supported by the structural data presented in Figures 5-6. The three distinct conformations are clearly demonstrated through structural comparisons, with quantitative measurements of movements provided. The identification of Structure II as a previously unseen open state with A-site tRNA is a significant finding supported by comparison with prior structures. The coupling of tRNA accommodation with 30S domain closure is clearly demonstrated.

result: The decoding center adopts distinct conformations in Structures II, III, and IV. In Structure II (open 30S), A1492 is inside helix 44 (OFF), G530 is separated from A1492 by >10 Å (OFF), and A1493 is bulged out but not stably interacting (ON). In Structure III (intermediate), A1493 and A1492 form A-minor interactions with the codon-anticodon helix (both ON), and G530 is shifted toward A1492 (SEMI-ON). In Structure IV (closed 30S), all decoding nucleotides adopt conformations identical to A-tRNA-bound ribosomes (A1493/A1492/G530 all ON), with G530 interacting with A1492.
evaluation: Claims C114-C122 are well-supported by the high-resolution cryo-EM density in the decoding center (Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplements 2-3). The progressive engagement of decoding center nucleotides is clearly demonstrated with sufficient local resolution to determine nucleotide conformations. The comparison with prior structures validates the assignments of open, intermediate, and closed states.

result: A structural mechanism for deacyl-tRNA decoding is proposed: at early steps, cognate or non-cognate tRNA interacts with the domain-open 30S conformation where decoding nucleotides are not positioned to stabilize the codon-anticodon helix. Non-cognate tRNA dissociates prior to 30S closure, while cognate tRNA acceptance and 30S domain closure are coupled with A1492-G530 bridge formation. The A1493-ON and A1493/A1492-ON states may serve as checkpoints for accepting Watson-Crick base-paired tRNA.
evaluation: Claims C123-C126, C95 propose a mechanistic model based on the structural data. While the structural observations (Structures II-IV) are well-supported, the proposed mechanism involves dynamic processes and discrimination between cognate and near-cognate tRNA that are not directly observed in the static structures. The model is reasonable and consistent with prior biochemical data (C93-C94), but lacks direct experimental validation of the proposed pathway. Additional kinetic or biochemical experiments would be needed to confirm this mechanism.

result: The N-terminal pseudo-hydrolase and synthetase domains show structural heterogeneity in Structures II-IV. Sub-classification revealed two predominant conformations differing by at least 10 Å, with additional classification suggesting a continuum of positions. In one conformation, the synthetase domain is positioned near the spur with a loop approaching within ~5 Å; in the other, it is shifted ~10 Å away. The pseudo-hydrolase domain is bound near the sarcin-ricin loop.
evaluation: Claims C78-C85 are supported by the sub-classification analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1. The structural heterogeneity is clearly demonstrated, and the two predominant conformations are resolved. However, the functional significance of these conformations and their relationship to catalytic activity remains uncertain, as acknowledged in the speculative claims C87-C88.

result: Multiple models for RelA activation are proposed: (1) conformational rearrangements between pseudo-hydrolase and synthetase domains triggered by movement or RNA interactions; (2) specific interactions of the synthetase domain with the spur; (3) RelA prepared for catalysis in all three states; (4) continuous transitions between states required; or (5) Structure IV alone is necessary for activation. The authors favor mechanisms requiring Structure IV with its accommodated cognate tRNA and closed decoding center.
evaluation: Claims C87-C88, C91, C153, C159-C161, C164 are speculative proposals about the activation mechanism. While based on structural observations (particularly the similarity to OAS1/cGAS activation mechanisms and the structural heterogeneity of N-terminal domains), these mechanisms are not directly tested. The preference for Structure IV as the activating state is reasonable given that near-cognate tRNAs don't trigger synthesis and likely don't reach the closed state, but this remains a hypothesis requiring biochemical validation.

result: The L11 N-terminus interacts with A/R tRNA but not with RelA in Structures II-IV. The lack of (p)ppGpp synthetase activity on mutant ribosomes missing L11 or its N-terminus is likely due to inability to coordinate deacyl-tRNA for RelA activation.
evaluation: Claims C34-C35 are supported by the structural data (Figure 1F-G, Figure 1—figure supplement 3) showing L11 N-terminus interactions with A/R tRNA. The interpretation that L11's role is in tRNA coordination rather than direct RelA interaction is a reasonable inference consistent with prior biochemical data (C33), though the mechanism could benefit from additional experimental validation.

result: Structure I shows that RelA can bind stalled ribosomes before deacyl-tRNA arrives, as the central and N-terminal domains are disordered in the absence of A-site tRNA. This indicates that tRNA presence is not necessary for RelA binding, but deacyl-tRNA binding is required to stabilize the extended RelA conformation.
evaluation: Claims C37, C157-C158 are supported by Structure I data (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A) showing ordered C-terminal domains but disordered N-terminal domains in the absence of A-site tRNA. This is consistent with prior biochemical observations (C18) and provides structural evidence for a binding mechanism where RelA can associate with ribosomes before tRNA arrival.

result: The RelA ACT domain interacts with double-stranded RNA via the same face that RNP domains use for single-stranded RNA binding. Linker helix 2 packs against the ACT domain similarly to the dimerization partner in isolated ACT domains, suggesting that ribosome binding requires ACT dimer disassembly. The A/R tRNA disrupts the TGS dimerization interface.
evaluation: Claims C44, C59-C60, C75 are supported by structural comparisons with isolated ACT and TGS domain structures (Figure 2D, Figure 3C). The inference that dimer disassembly is required for ribosome binding is reasonable based on the structural incompatibility, though direct evidence of RelA dimerization in solution and its disruption upon ribosome binding would strengthen this conclusion.

result: Structural comparisons show that early elongation steps are compatible with ribosome-bound but inactive RelA, as EF-Tu ternary complex does not clash with RelA C-terminal domains. However, full tRNA accommodation and translocation would require RelA displacement, as the ACT domain clashes with accommodated A-site tRNA, and EF-G binding (both rotated and non-rotated states) is incompatible with RelA binding.
evaluation: Claims C138-C146 are supported by structural superpositions with EF-Tu and EF-G complexes (Figure 7—figure supplement 1). The steric clash analyses are clearly demonstrated. This provides a structural explanation for why RelA must be displaced during active translation, consistent with prior biochemical observations (C137, C142). The inference that RelA cannot be activated during translation is well-supported.

result: A bifactorial mechanism of RelA activation is proposed: (1) stabilization in the 70S•deacyl-tRNA complex alleviates autoinhibition by disrupting ACT and TGS dimerization surfaces through AH domain ordering and CCA end interaction; (2) conformational changes in N-terminal domains and/or spur interactions activate the synthetase. During normal translation, aminoacyl-tRNA accommodation and translocation displace RelA from bridge B1a, limiting (p)ppGpp production.
evaluation: Claims C147-C149, C151-C152, C154, C156 propose an activation mechanism based on structural observations and comparison with isolated domain structures. While the structural basis for autoinhibition relief (dimer disruption) is reasonable, it remains speculative as the oligomeric state of free RelA and its disruption upon ribosome binding are not directly demonstrated. The model is consistent with prior biochemical data and the structures, but requires additional biochemical validation to be fully supported.

result: The RelA synthetase domain structure resembles other second-messenger synthetases including OAS1, cGAS, and DncV. OAS1 and cGAS are activated by binding RNA or DNA duplexes at the spine helix.
evaluation: Claims C89-C90 are supported by structural comparisons shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 2, with appropriate citations to prior structural work. The structural similarity is clearly demonstrated and provides context for understanding potential activation mechanisms.

result: The observation of previously elusive tRNA binding states suggests insights into aminoacyl-tRNA selection during elongation. The tRNA acceptor arm positions are separated by ~5 Å between early (Structure II) and closed (Structure IV) states, potentially keeping EF-Tu farther from the GTPase-activating sarcin-ricin loop at early steps, allowing non-cognate ternary complex dissociation before GTP hydrolysis.
evaluation: Claims C127, C131-C133 extrapolate from the RelA-bound structures to propose insights into aminoacyl-tRNA selection during normal elongation. While the structural observations are valid, the relevance to EF-Tu-mediated tRNA selection is speculative. The authors acknowledge (end of C133) that further structural and biochemical studies of aminoacyl-tRNA•EF-Tu•GTP complexes are needed to test whether the mechanisms are similar.

result: The extended RelA conformation observed in this study contrasts with a compact conformation proposed from a prior 10.8-Å map, but re-evaluation of that lower-resolution map reveals previously unassigned density near bridge B1a consistent with the extended conformation.
evaluation: Claims C53-C54 are supported by the re-analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2. This reconciles the current high-resolution structures with prior lower-resolution work (C24-C26), demonstrating that the extended conformation is consistent with earlier data when properly interpreted.

result: Two subsequently published studies reported RelA-bound structures with ATP analog and GTP (substrate-bound states), while this work describes substrate-free states. Both studies noted conformational variability consistent with these observations. Differences in predominant conformations may be due to paromomycin use, substrate analogs, or methodological differences.
evaluation: Claims C166-C169 appropriately contextualize this work relative to subsequently published studies. The distinction between substrate-free (this work) and substrate-bound states is clearly stated. The speculation about reasons for differences (C169) is reasonable, though the authors appropriately acknowledge uncertainty about the exact causes.

result: Background claims about stringent response, RelA function, domain organization, and prior biochemical/structural knowledge are established from the literature.
evaluation: These claims (C1-C3, C10-C23, C33, C72, C76, C93-C94, C112-C113, C128-C129, C134-C137, C162) represent established knowledge from prior research, appropriately cited throughout the manuscript. They provide necessary context for interpreting the new structural findings.
